description: We are Group 12ki, studying at the Separated Structural Subdivision "Applied College of Yuriy Fedkovych Chernivtsi National University."
summary: LIFE BOT is an intelligent operating system designed to support the life, coordination, and safety of crew members during space missions. The project combines six main modules: physical health monitoring, mental health monitoring, crew location tracking, secure communication, emergency SOS alerts, and system configuration. LIFE BOT enables the monitoring of astronauts’ vital signs, early detection of potential risks, assessment of psychological well-being, and rapid coordination in critical situations. The system also facilitates information exchange between crew members and mission control. The project aims to improve astronaut safety, reduce risks, and enhance the team’s operational efficiency. This is particularly important because, during long-duration space missions, even a minor health or communication issue can affect the success of the entire expedition.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

LifeBot is a desktop application, offline, that combines the physical, psychological and spacesuit health of an astronaut into a single dashboard. It's a working prototype which operates on simulation data.

- Physical monitoring. Crew profile and telemetry including heart rate, blood pressure and temperature is displayed and updated every minute. Blood pressure is classified in line with USA Heart Association and NHS references. Simple threshold rules will trigger alerts when a value is deemed to be unusual.
- Psychological monitoring. There is no automated psychological analysis. Astronauts self-rate their stress and concentration levels (0-100), hours slept (0-24) and mood (1-5). History keeps to allow changes to be viewed over time.
- Spacesuit monitoring. The interface displays suit parameters (integrity, oxygen level, temperature, pressure and life-support status). The values are synthetic values for now, but the design will be open to being integrated with real suit sensor values in the future.
- JARVIS assistant. A local rule based assistant, JARVIS, is implemented, not a language connected model. Reads crew profiles, telemetry and self-assessments from a local sqlite database and responds to typed queries regarding crew status, an individual's readings, anomalies, diagnostics. History of conversations stored on the local computer. No voice control, no external AI service is called at run-time.

All data and JARVIS' history remain on the device, so that the application can also be used offline.

What are the benefits of the project?

- One location for health and safety. Typically, physical well-being is not a concern of mental state, or suit condition. LifeBot presents them all together, which means that an astronaut or controller can view the entire situation at a glance.
- Mental health included. The stress factors of isolation, confined space and workload are known in spaceflight. LifeBot treats them the same as vital signs.
- Quick Information retrieval. This is JARVIS that enables one to ask a question and get an answer without navigating screens.
- Works offline. Requires no Internet or cloud connection – perfect for missions with poor or intermittent communications.
- Complements existing systems. It is intended as an additional module which will complement existing monitoring solutions, not supplant them.
- Readable design. The user interface is designed to be easy to understand, and significant details are emphasized.

What is the expected impact?

We do not regard LifeBot as the end of the line for medical products, but rather a stepping stone to additional tools for crew care in the future. It is in its current form, demonstrating the integration of physical, psychological and equipment data into one light-weight, offline tool.

With further development (real sensor integration, validated alert logic, secure data handling), it could:

- improve the detection of concerning trends before crews and mission control, and
- put mental well-being on the same level as physical health in mission monitoring,
- provide assistance for crew-and-ground cooperation for long duration missions, such as the Moon and Mars.

Concepts can be applied to other isolated or extreme environments such as Polar stations, submarines, aviation and rescue teams. These are potential users only - they are not actual users. There is no restriction on access and no network sync/connection to real systems in the current version.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages and frameworks: C++ and Qt (desktop application and interface).
Data storage: SQLite (local database for profiles, telemetry, self-assessments and JARVIS history).
Design: Figma (interface design).
Development assistance: We used AI tools (Claude, Codex, ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Gemini) to support development. They helped us build the project but are not part of the application. LifeBot does not call any AI API at runtime.
Hardware: None. The prototype runs on a standard computer with simulated data. Connecting wearable and suit sensors is a future step.
Reference sources: AHA and NHS materials for blood pressure categories, and NASA publications on behavioral health, spacesuit incidents and human integration design.

How creative is your project?

Mind and suit in one tool. The majority of monitoring concepts are limited to vital signs. LifeBot combines physical health, psychological state and condition of the spacesuit into one package and considers the suit to be a component of the astronaut's life-support system.
Mental health as a first-class feature. Psychological wellbeing is measured in parallel with the physical wellbeing, not as an extra dimension.
Offline-first assistant. JARVIS is not a cloud AI, it is a simple, local assistant. It connects without signal and stores crew data on the device, and can subsequently be upgraded to a more powerful version.
Module, not replacement. It's developed to be an enhancement to the already available systems and therefore there is the possibility of a slow adoption.

What were some of the factors your team took into account?

Usability under stress. The interface is easy to read, visually pleasing and indicates important information; seconds can count during emergencies.
Connectivity. Core functions operate in an offline mode as communication with Earth can be interrupted or delayed.
Local storage for privacy. No external AI service is used and data remains on the device.
Compatibility. The modular concept allows LifeBot to connect with other monitoring applications.
Honest limitations. We critically looked at the prototype and determined what is necessary for it to be used:
- Data security: No data is encrypted in the database and there is no separation of access between crew and medical staff, no access log and no rules governing data deletion. NASA has a medical records protection policy.
- Connectivity: When a connection returns, there is no reliable sync. NASA's delay tolerant networking approach can be used as a model.
- Power: Power The Telemetry update is once a minute, but the heart-rate graph has an animation timer of 40 ms giving us no chance of saying the app is battery efficient just yet.
- Alert reliability: Alerts are based on simple thresholds and may be based on one abnormal value. No multi-measurement check, personal baseline or signal quality assessment. NASA says that excessive warnings can cause people to disregard them — that's a top priority for improvement.
- Medical status: Results shown reflect self-evaluations or synthetic data, not a diagnosis or specialist's conclusion. LifeBot is a prototype for demonstration purposes only and is not a validated medical decision or flight system.
